title: The AI governance question every leadership team should be asking
summary: Unisys CEO Mike Thomson on why AI governance can't wait for policy to catch up, what a governance framework requires, and how leaders can get ahead of it.
body_markdown:
#### Short on time? Read the key takeaways:


- Governance has to move at the same speed as adoption, or people will find ways around whatever policy does exist.
- An effective governance framework should cover at least three things: which tools and models are approved, who can access which data and under what conditions, and a decision process fast enough to keep pace with the technology and emerging regulatory requirements.
- Data and IP leakage giving your secret sauce to competitors are immediate exposures every leadership team should plan for.
- Build governance into technology rollouts from day one, before usage outpaces it.


#### By the time many leadership teams sit down to write an AI policy, people in their organizations may already have been using AI for months, sometimes years, without one.


Someone found a[use for a tool](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/artificial-intelligence/#solutionOverview) , the value was obvious, and adoption spread before anyone decided how it should be used, what data it could touch, or what happens when something goes wrong. Sound familiar?


Here's the question worth sitting with: do you know how the AI already active in your organization is being used, and are you comfortable with the answer? Most leadership teams think the decision still ahead of them is whether to allow a given tool, but that call has usually already been made by their own people.


That's a realistic pattern for technology: value moves first, and governance follows. The gap in between, however long it lasts, is where the exposure sits for every organization moving at this pace.


At Unisys, we paired access with guardrails as we scaled our[own AI adoption](https://www.unisys.com/our-clients/human-centered-ai/) . When new tools went out to our workforce, so did the rules on data handling and acceptable use, at the same time, as one decision instead of two. That's the model I'd offer any leadership team: design speed and governance together, and you won't be stuck choosing between them later. That's easier said than built, so here's what it takes in practice: what a governance framework has to cover, what skipping it costs, and why it doesn't stay internal for long.


### It's not just an internal problem


Our commercial team regularly hears a version of this story from clients. Early AI conversations were about getting started. They aren't anymore. Now, a client will tell us they have[hundreds or thousands of AI agents](https://www.unisys.com/blog-post/cis/agentic-ai-is-giving-application-managed-services-new-life-heres-how/) already running and then ask: Are they well-built? Are they tested? Are they governed? Are they even structured in a way anyone can track?


That's the question organizations eventually face once pilots become large-scale deployments. Underneath the technology question lies a governance question. The tools are easy enough to deploy, but that deployment can outrun oversight.


The same problem shows up around[data access](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/cai/data-analytics/) . When we ask clients what limits their AI programs, the answer is rarely a shortage of use cases. It's governed, structured data, and clear rules on who's allowed to touch it. That's close to a universal bottleneck at this point. Easier tools don't make that problem disappear. They just make it show up faster.


### What a governance framework has to cover


An effective governance framework has to do three things well.


1. **It has to set tooling standards** : which models and platforms are approved, and why, so nobody has to guess, or default to whatever tool is already open on their screen.
2. **It has to set[data access controls](https://www.unisys.com/announcements-and-updates/cis/unisys-and-microsoft-partner-to-deliver-integrated-data-governance-and-management/)** : who can connect what to which systems, under what conditions, and with what data those systems can share back out.
3. **And it has to run on a decision process** fast enough to keep up with how technology moves, and emerging AI regulations evolve.


We operate on the principle that governance escalations should be resolved in hours or days, not weeks or months. A framework that can't move at that speed will be bypassed, because the pace of the technology won't wait for it. At that point, you don't have governance. You have a policy nobody follows.


### What it costs to skip this


Frontier AI models raise concerns around data and intellectual property leakage. In some cases, the same providers that a company shares information with gain enough visibility into that business to build competing products of their own. Add development tools that put new capabilities directly into employees’ hands, and the[attack surface](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/cai/cybersecurity/) grows with every deployment a company adds. None of that is an argument for slowing AI adoption down. It's an argument for governance moving at the same pace as adoption, so the two never drift far apart.


### Getting ahead of it


Build governance into the rollout itself, on the same timeline as the tools, rather than adding restrictive policies after the fact. A program like that is simple to describe, even if it's hard to build. Everyone in the organization understands the policies, knows the do's and don'ts of using AI, and knows how to keep themselves and the company safe. Operationalization should also align governance and compliance with the legal requirements taking shape worldwide. That's the bar I'd set for any AI governance program, including our own.


Building that framework is exactly the kind of work our[AI consulting team](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/consulting/) helps organizations do, setting tooling standards, building data access controls, and putting a decision-making process in place that keeps pace with technology and the regulatory environment. If your organization is still working out where governance fits into its AI rollout, that's a conversation worth having with us.

## FAQs


AI governance is the set of policies, controls, and decision processes that determine which AI tools are approved, how data can be used with them, and who is accountable when something goes wrong. It matters because adoption almost always spreads before policy does, and that gap is where risk builds up.


Because the value of a new tool is typically obvious to the people using it long before any formal review catches up. That's a normal pattern for fast-moving, useful technology, rather than a sign of poor discipline. It just means governance has to be built to intentionally close the gap.


Three things: tooling standards for which models and platforms are approved, data access controls that define who can connect to which systems, and a decision process fast enough, ideally resolved in hours or days, to keep pace with how quickly the technology and regulatory environment changes.


Data and intellectual property leakage, and in some cases, the same AI providers that a company shares information with become competitors in that company's own market. Development tools that put capability directly into employees' hands also widen the attack surface with every new deployment.


By deciding on tooling standards and data access rules at the same time new tools go out, not months afterward, and by building a decision process fast enough that people never have a reason to work around it.
